title: How to Rodent Proof Your Attic
h1: How Do You Rodent Proof an Attic?
description: How to rodent proof an attic: where rats and mice get in, how to seal entry points, safe cleanup of droppings and insulation, and keeping them out for good.
quick_answer: Rodent proofing an attic means finding and sealing every gap a mouse or rat can squeeze through, removing the rodents already inside, then cleaning up droppings and contaminated insulation. Focus on roof and eave gaps, vents, pipe and wire openings, and tree branches touching the roof. Use metal mesh or hardware cloth, not foam alone.
body:
How do rodents get into attics?

Roof rats are common in San Diego and Orange County. They're good climbers and travel along fences, utility lines, palm trees and overhanging branches to reach the roof. Mice get in lower and climb through walls. Both fit through surprisingly small openings.

The usual entry points are:

  • Gaps where the roof meets the eaves or fascia
  • Damaged or loose roof, gable and soffit vent screens
  • Openings around plumbing vents, AC line sets, cable and electrical lines
  • Gaps at the corners of the roof and where rooflines meet
  • Broken or missing roof tiles and gaps under tile edges
  • Garage door gaps and openings into the garage attic

What are the signs of rodents in the attic?

  • Scratching or scurrying noises at night
  • Droppings in the attic, garage or along walls
  • Tunnels and nests in the insulation
  • Chewed wiring, ducts or stored items
  • Grease marks along beams and around openings
  • A musty or ammonia smell, sometimes noticeable through the vents

You might also notice pets staring at the ceiling or a sudden increase in dust and odors from the vents. Rodents are most active at night, so listen in the late evening and early morning.

Chewed flex ducts are a common find. Once rodents tear into a duct, the system can pull attic air and debris directly into the house.

How do you seal an attic against rodents?

  1. Inspect inside and out. Walk the roofline and check from the attic for daylight coming through gaps.
  2. Remove the rodents first. Sealing them in creates a bigger problem. Trapping works better than poison in an attic, since poisoned rodents often die inside walls or insulation.
  3. Seal openings with durable materials. Use galvanized hardware cloth, metal flashing, or copper or steel mesh. Spray foam alone gets chewed through quickly.
  4. Repair vent screens with heavy metal mesh so the attic still ventilates.
  5. Seal utility penetrations where lines enter the house or attic.
  6. Trim trees and vines back from the roof so rodents can't jump on.

How do you clean up after rodents safely?

Rodent droppings and urine can carry diseases, and disturbing them can put particles in the air. Don't sweep or vacuum droppings dry. Health guidance calls for wetting them with a disinfectant first, wearing gloves and a well-fitted mask, and bagging the waste.

In an attic, the bigger job is usually the insulation. Insulation that's full of droppings, urine and nesting material can't really be cleaned. It should be removed, the attic sanitized, and fresh insulation installed. That also gets rid of the odors that can attract new rodents.

Should you do it yourself or hire a pro?

Trimming branches, picking up fruit and setting traps in the garage are reasonable homeowner tasks. Working on the roof edge, sealing gaps at the eaves, and removing contaminated insulation are harder and riskier jobs. Attic floors aren't designed to walk on between the joists, and attics in summer get dangerously hot. A crew that does this regularly knows where rats in our area tend to get in and has the equipment to clean up safely.

How do you keep rodents from coming back?

Rodent proofing isn't a one-time thing. Roofs settle, vent screens get damaged and new utility lines get run. A few habits help:

  • Keep tree branches and palm fronds trimmed back from the roof.
  • Pick up fallen fruit from citrus and avocado trees.
  • Store pet food and birdseed in sealed containers.
  • Keep firewood and clutter away from the house.
  • Check the attic once or twice a year for fresh droppings or damage.

Should you replace attic insulation after a rodent problem?

In most cases, yes, if the insulation has a lot of droppings, urine staining or nests. Contaminated insulation holds odors and loses insulating value when it's matted. Replacing it is also a good time to check and repair any chewed ducts and wiring.

After the cleanup, sealing the attic floor and adding fresh insulation leaves you with a cleaner, more comfortable attic than before the rodents moved in.

faqs: What size hole can a rat or mouse fit through?

Smaller than most people expect. Mice can squeeze through gaps about the width of a pencil, and rats through holes about the size of a quarter. Any opening a rodent can get its head into is worth sealing.
Can I use spray foam to block rodent entry points?
Spray foam alone isn't enough because rodents chew through it. Use galvanized hardware cloth, metal flashing or steel or copper mesh, and add foam or sealant behind it to close air gaps if needed.
Is it safe to go into an attic with rodent droppings?

Brief inspections are fine with gloves and a well-fitted mask, but avoid stirring up droppings. Don't sweep or vacuum them dry. Large cleanups, especially those involving insulation removal, are best handled by a professional crew with proper protective equipment.
Do rodents damage HVAC ducts in the attic?

Yes, often. Rodents chew through flex duct to nest or reach warm air. Damaged ducts leak conditioned air and can pull droppings and insulation into the system. Ducts should be inspected and repaired or replaced after a rodent problem.
